questions.q: Why does this lesson say the schema-design bar is 'higher' for an action tool than a read-only tool, even though both use the same Messages API shape?
options: Action tools use a completely different JSON format
A poorly-described read-only tool wastes a turn if called wrong; a poorly-described action tool does something real
Read-only tools don't need a description at all
There is no actual difference in the stakes
questions.explain: The description discipline from the AI Agents course doesn't change, but the consequence of a vague or ambiguous description is far more serious once the tool can actually act.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does issue_refund's description require that look_up_order run first?
options: Because the Messages API enforces tool call ordering automatically
So the refund is only issued after the order and its paid amount have been confirmed, rather than guessed
Because look_up_order and issue_refund share the same input_schema
It's not actually required -- the description just mentions it in passing
questions.explain: The description explicitly states the refund should only happen after look_up_order confirms the order and amount, reducing the chance of refunding the wrong order or an incorrect amount.

questions.q: Where does the requires_approval flag for a tool live, according to this lesson?
options: Inside the tool's input_schema, as a required field
In the tool's name, as a prefix
In the application's own metadata, alongside the tool definition but not sent to Claude as part of the schema
It is set automatically by the Messages API based on the tool's description length
questions.explain: requires_approval is explicitly called out as an app-level flag, not part of the Anthropic tool schema -- your own code checks it before deciding whether to run the approval workflow.

questions.q: What is the practical benefit of classifying each tool's risk tier at design time, before Lesson 15's approval workflow is built?
options: It makes the tool descriptions shorter
It lets the approval checkpoint simply check a flag already set, instead of inferring risk from a tool call after the fact
It removes the need for any approval workflow at all
It is purely a documentation exercise with no effect on the code
questions.explain: Deciding risk tiers up front means the approval logic in Lesson 15 is a straightforward flag check rather than fragile runtime guesswork about how risky a given call might be.

questions.q: In the worked support-ticket example, which tool is read-only and therefore does not require approval?
options: issue_refund
look_up_order
Both tools require approval
Neither tool requires approval
questions.explain: look_up_order only retrieves information and makes no changes, so it's classified as read-only with no approval requirement, unlike the irreversible issue_refund.
